title: Walking and Shoes in Eighteenth-Century London

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It was difficult to get about in eighteenth-century London. During the first half of that century, the physical mobility of the upper classes in the city had been considerably restricted: the poor condition of the streets did not allow 'walking for pleasure' outside private parks or pleasure gardens. Streets were dirty, rubbish was everywhere and the British climate did not help. Walking could be a risky business. The terrible state of roads, always flooded and muddy, created a metropolitan world of shoe cleaners and street sweepers.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: References to walking are not abundant in early eighteenth-century texts. This is truer for urban spaces than for places in the countryside, where country life had always been dominated by a lifestyle of outdoor activities. For instance, in eighteenth-century London, a sightseer’s experience was restricted to touristic places and involved journeys by a series of boats and coaches. Walking was considered to be an activity for the poorer members of society – or simply those who could not afford a coach.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This situation underwent a sudden improvement in the mid-eighteenth century, with measures implementing the provision of public spaces in which to walk. The first legislation concerning paving in London was passed in 1762, and during the following decades, similar laws were enacted in many cities. By the end of the century, areas for walking were commonplace and far more people were enjoying the pastime than before. Sophie von la Roche writes about metropolitan street life in the diary of her visit to London of 1786. She comments on how many more pedestrians there were on the broad, clean pavements, alongside the houses where, she says, 'many thousands of neatly clad people, eminent men and dressy women, pursue their way safe from the carriages, horses and dirt'. Although the pastime of walking was pursued only in specific spaces designed for the purpose, the number of these spaces increased as the nineteenth century approached. Travelling on foot became smoother and less dangerous.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Attitudes toward walking through public spaces and their changes over time were visible in the practical designs of fashionable footwear. Protective overshoes and other devices designed to keep feet above the dirty and wet ground soon disappeared, and ease of mobility increased. In the early eighteenth century, the look of men's and women's shoes started to diverge in appearance as a distinction between male and female footwear filtered into production. Contemporary descriptions of the boot and shoe trade underlined the differences between ladies' shoemakers and men's shoemakers, too.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The production of men's and women's footwear required different skills, as the products were essentially different. Men wore more sober footwear, not unlike modern shoes. Their shoes were entirely made of leather, which provided resistance to rain, mud and bad weather. Women's shoes had uppers made of textiles – silk, satin or cloth – and their resistance to bad weather and dirty streets was limited. Only the lower ranks of women wore leather shoes of a form similar to men's. The high-quality shoes for women were often embroidered and were normally worn with protective overshoes, as they were prone to being damaged or disfigured by the conditions of the time.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The shoes of men and women related to their more general clothing in different ways. Wealthy women's footwear harmonised with their other garments, a harmony that could be effected through matching textiles, general colour, embroidered detail, or buckles. In the eighteenth century, men's shoes matched their clothing in different ways, for example with glossy black, red or pink heels. The shoe of an upper-class man also acted as a type of sign which emphasised the difference between the wearer and young boys and women. The shoe also distinguished him from working men who wore leather or cloth protective leggings, into ragged shoes and clogs. The symbolic marking of the entry of a wealthy young man into manhood through his shoes, as well as his other dress, may have been of more importance than has previously been acknowledged in costume history.
